tools.title: Git LFS + File Locking Workflow
tools.summary: Store .uasset/.umap in Git LFS and lock binary assets that cannot be merged safely.
workflow: Track .uasset/.umap with LFS.
Mark them lockable.
Lock before edit.
Pull/rebase before work.
Unlock after successful push.
Never attempt text merges of binary assets.
tools.codex: Before mutating a binary asset, verify repository cleanliness and lock/ownership policy; never auto-force conflicts.
tools.caution: LFS alone does not prevent merge conflicts; locking discipline matters.

tools.title: Project Borealis UEGitPlugin
tools.summary: Refactored Unreal Git/LFS source-control provider with file locking and status-branch workflow improvements.
workflow: Evaluate on a disposable UE 5.8 project first.
Use HTTPS/Git Credential Manager.
Adopt explicit .gitattributes.
Keep CLI Git as the source-of-truth fallback.
tools.codex: Useful if the team wants editor-native locks, but Codex can operate Git from CLI without requiring this plugin.
tools.caution: Open issues report compatibility/usability problems in newer UE versions; do not make it mandatory until tested on 5.8.

tools.title: Unreal Commandlets in CI
tools.summary: Run validation, resave, cook and other editor operations headlessly through UnrealEditor-Cmd/commandlets.
workflow: Start with DataValidation commandlet.
Add targeted project commandlets only for deterministic tasks.
Fail CI on errors.
Archive logs/reports.
tools.codex: Codex should produce CI commands alongside new validators/tools so every guardrail is automatable.
tools.caution: Headless/commandlet execution can differ from interactive editor paths; test both where relevant.

tools.title: BuildGraph
tools.summary: Epic's XML-based build orchestration layer on top of Unreal Automation Tool.
workflow: Keep BuildGraph scripts in source control.
Separate build, test, cook and publish nodes.
Parameterize platform/configuration.
Run on dedicated build machines.
tools.codex: Codex can update BuildGraph definitions when project build/test requirements change.
tools.caution: Start simple; do not build an enterprise pipeline before the project needs it.

tools.title: Clean Build / Cook / Package Verification
tools.summary: Regularly validate the project outside the warm developer editor: clean build, cook and package.
workflow: Run clean Editor build periodically.
Cook target platforms.
Package Development/Shipping candidates.
Launch packaged build.
Run smoke/automation tests.
tools.codex: A task is not release-ready merely because PIE works; Codex should report clean build/cook/package status separately.
tools.caution: Live Coding success is insufficient evidence for release readiness.

tools.title: Horde
tools.summary: Epic infrastructure for build automation, remote execution, test automation, studio analytics and device farms.
workflow: Start only when project/team scale justifies dedicated infrastructure.
Pilot Horde locally or on a small server.
Connect agents and one build/test stream.
Add auth, observability and resource pools before broader rollout.
tools.codex: Codex can author BuildGraph/Horde config and inspect logs/results, but infrastructure changes should remain reviewed.
tools.caution: Horde is powerful and operationally heavier than a simple Azure/GitHub pipeline; do not adopt merely because it exists.

tools.title: Unreal Build Accelerator (UBA)
tools.summary: Accelerates C++ compilation locally and, with Horde, can distribute build actions across remote machines.
why: Reduces iteration time on large C++ codebases
Remote compilation can use otherwise idle machines
Especially useful once full editor builds become a productivity bottleneck
workflow: Measure local clean/incremental build times first.
Enable/tune UBA using UBT configuration.
For remote acceleration, configure Horde agents and secure access.
Track build reliability and speed before expanding the pool.
tools.codex: Codex can inspect BuildConfiguration and build logs, but should not alter distributed-build infrastructure without an explicit task.
tools.caution: Remote build support/platform details evolve by engine release; follow the exact UE 5.8 documentation and secure Horde authentication.

tools.title: Azure DevOps CI for Unreal
tools.priority: High when Azure hosts the game repo
tools.summary: Use an Azure Pipelines self-hosted build machine with Unreal installed to run validation, UBT/UAT, cook, package and test jobs.
why: Keeps the Unreal build environment under your control
Machine-level engine/cache state persists across jobs
Fits Azure Repos and branch policies
Can publish packaged builds/test artifacts automatically
workflow: Provision a dedicated self-hosted Windows agent with the exact Unreal version/toolchain.
Checkout Git LFS correctly.
Run lightweight validation first, then UBT/UAT build/cook/test stages.
Cache/use shared DDC where appropriate.
Publish logs, test reports and packaged artifacts; gate protected branches on required jobs.
tools.codex: Codex can author/maintain azure-pipelines.yml and project build scripts, while engine credentials/signing secrets stay in secure variables.
tools.caution: Microsoft-hosted agents are usually a poor fit for large Unreal builds because the engine/toolchain/cache is heavy; prefer self-hosted agents for repeatable production builds.

tools.title: Multi-User Editing
tools.summary: Connects multiple Unreal Editor instances into a shared live editing session for real-time collaborative content work.
why: Multiple people can work together in the same world
Useful for review sessions, level dressing and collaborative iteration
Works on top of a defined source-control revision
workflow: Make every participant sync the exact same project revision and engine version.
Launch/join a short-lived Multi-User session on LAN/VPN.
Collaborate live.
At session end, persist and commit the agreed changes through normal source control.
tools.codex: Mostly a human collaboration tool; Codex should understand that the live session does not replace source control and should avoid conflicting automated writes during a session.
tools.caution: Epic explicitly positions Multi-User Editing as an addition to source control, not a replacement. Keep sessions short-lived and start from the same revision.

tools.title: One File Per Actor (OFPA)
tools.summary: Stores level Actor instance data in external files so different team members can modify different Actors without constantly touching the main level file.
why: Reduces source-control contention on large levels
Enabled by default with World Partition
Makes parallel world editing more practical
Cooked builds still embed Actors normally
workflow: Use World Partition or enable OFPA for the target level.
Keep actor edits scoped and review source-control changes carefully.
Use locks/source-control discipline for assets that remain indivisible.
Validate level load/cook after large structural changes.
tools.codex: When editing level actors, Codex should understand OFPA-generated files as engine-owned content and avoid renaming/manipulating them directly on disk.
tools.caution: OFPA helps actor-level contention but does not make arbitrary .uasset files mergeable.

tools.title: Unreal Collaboration Strategy: Git LFS + Locks + Short-Lived Branches
tools.summary: A practical team policy for binary Unreal content: LFS storage, explicit locks for non-mergeable assets, small branches and frequent synchronization.
why: Keeps binary history out of normal Git object storage
Makes ownership of currently edited assets visible
workflow: Track Unreal binary assets with Git LFS before adding them.
Lock high-conflict binary assets before editing.
Pull/rebase before starting significant asset work.
Keep branches/tasks narrow and integrate frequently.
Never resolve a binary merge by guessing; choose one asset revision or merge using Unreal-aware tooling when supported.
tools.codex: Before modifying binary assets, Codex should inspect source-control status/locks and avoid parallel edits to the same asset.
tools.caution: LFS does not make binary assets mergeable. Coordination and locking remain necessary.
